question: Can God be seen?
summary: The Hebrew Bible repeatedly narrates theophanies in which God is seen face-to-face — by Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, seventy elders, Manoah, Micaiah, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Habakkuk. A parallel stream (Exod 33:20; John 1:18; 1 Tim 6:16; Col 1:15) insists God is invisible and cannot be seen, and that anyone who did see him would die. Scripture affirms both mutually exclusive positions without resolving them.

reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish kinds of seeing — God's symbolic or partial manifestation, and "seen" used for "known" — from a literal sight of his invisible essence.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, compiler of the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, presses that Scripture both narrates God being seen face to face and flatly states no one can see God and live.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Exodus 33:20
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact tension on Exod 33:20: the unveiled glory cannot be seen in the present mortal state, while 'men have, in a sense, seen the face of God in this life, and have lived' — distinguishing the senses against the death-on-seeing notion (citing Gen 32:30).

link.title: GotQuestions: If Moses met face to face with God, why, later, was he not allowed to see God's face?

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: No man hath seen God at any time — Moses and others heard his voice, and saw the cloud and the fire, which were the symbols of his presence; but such a manifestation of God as had now taken place, in the person of Jesus Christ, had never before been exhibited to the world. It is likely that the word seen, here, is put for known …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles the seeing/not-seeing tension: prior figures perceived only symbols of God's presence (cloud, fire, voice), not God himself, and 'seen' carries the sense 'fully known' — so John 1:18 does not contradict the theophanies. Single strongest harmonization, parity-capped against the lone named skeptic.
excerpts.source_note_text:
No man hath seen God at any time - Moses and others heard his voice, and saw the cloud and the fire, which were the symbols of his presence; but such a manifestation of God as had now taken place, in the person of Jesus Christ, had never before been exhibited to the world. It is likely that the word seen, here, is put for known, as in Joh 3:32; Jo1 3:2, Jo1 3:6, and Jo3 1:11; and this sense the latter clause of the verse seems to require: - No man, how highly soever favored, hath fully known God, at any time, in any nation or age; the only begotten Son, (see on Joh 1:14 (note)), who is in the bosom of the Father, who was intimately acquainted with all the counsels of the Most High, he hath declared him, εξηγησατο, hath announced the Divine oracles unto men; for in this sense the word is used by the best Greek writers. See Kypke in loco.
Lying in the bosom, is spoken of in reference to the Asiatic custom of reclining while at meals; the person who was next the other was said to lie in his bosom; and he who had this place in reference to the master of the feast was supposed to share his peculiar regards, and so be in a state of the utmost favor and intimacy with him.
